newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - John Tesh - music is entertainment tonight.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - John Tesh - music is entertainment tonight.

text.p: For those who cannot stand him and think his music is mush, John Tesh has a simple answer: So what?
"I would rather be hated and vilified than ignored," said the lanky pianist and former anchor of the syndicated TV show "Entertainment Tonight."

"It hurt me more when I got slammed for doing the Olympics last year," he said of his stint covering gymnastics and other sports in Atlanta for NBC television. "Some reviewers said 'What's the host of ET doing there?' and 'It's much too dramatic.' That hurt me more than any of the music jibes and I had no way of defending myself.

"I couldn't go on the air and say 'Screw you guys,' but when you get slammed on a Monday after a Sunday concert and Monday night you're playing in front of 10,000 people, it's gratification," he said.
Tesh has good reason to give a symbolic finger to the critical barbs from the music press over his bland pop instrumentals -- hundreds of thousands of people buy his albums and flock to his concerts.

His 1995 album "Live at Red Rocks" went gold, selling more than 800,000 copies, and the video of that concert shown on Public Broadcasting stations was responsible for PBS' best-ever fund-raising efforts.
He has released nine solo albums and four group efforts and won four Emmys for his compositions for sports events. His "Roundball Rock" is the signature tune for NBC telecasts of basketball games.
GOES BEYOND THE STARS

Not bad for someone best known by most TV viewers as the blond guy who sat next to Mary Hart on Entertainment Tonight, reading puff stories about the stars for 10 years. That was a cushy job, he admits, but last year he walked away from ET to concentrate on his first love -- music.
"I have nothing against the show and they were great to me and my music. But I just felt like I was always in a hurry," Tesh told Reuters in a recent interview.
"People probably say 'Gee, poor John,' but by the same token I gave up a seven-figure job," he said. "You just don't need that much cash.

"I felt I was doing too much, when people are offering you talk shows and you say 'Yeah, I can do that.' I used to be one of those people who reached for (daily) Variety and had to read it through before I could drink my morning coffee to see what everybody else was doing."

Asked if his strong Christian faith played a role in helping him walk away from such a high-profile TV job, Tesh became animated. "Faith? Definitely, oh gosh. About deciding whether to leave ET? Oh big time. ... I don't have to worry. I have three things to concentrate on -- being a husband, being a dad and being a musician."

Tesh, Long Island-born and raised a Baptist, is married to actress Connie Selleca. They are members of a Messianic church -- "A great mix of Old and New Testament," he said, adding that his record company is located in the church building.

"I make no secret of the fact that I am Christian. I don't believe in crystals or false idols or mysticism or anything like that and I don't worship astrologers," he said, alluding to critics who think of him as a New Age performer.

"I would sooner describe the music we perform as pop instrumentals than New Age," he said of his music that combines elements of rock and jazz with melodic piano solos, all augmented with strings and saxophones.
BIG ROCK FAN

Raised on rock (Emerson, Lake and Palmer, Jethro Tull and Yes are among his favourite bands) but classically trained, Tesh has cultivated an audience he says stretches from 30-year-olds to 75 and beyond.

It was while doing a stint in the 1980's with CBS Sports covering the Tour de France bicycle race that his music first came to the fore. He composed and performed soundtracks for race footage and viewers bombarded the network asking where they could buy it. He eventually sold 30,000 copies of the tape, selling them out of his garage.
The passionate devotion of his fans can be seen in his new album and video "Avalon" -- recorded at a concert in Avalon on the island of Catalina off the southern California coast.
And what if there are more snide reviews?

"It's not like it's something I want to happen but there's a fair amount of people out there that are buying records and coming to concerts. If the reviewers were killing me and no one was embracing the music, then I'd be a news reader," Tesh said with a laugh.
